title: Commission rules officer justified in shooting death of Kevin St. Arnaud
article: The Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP has found Const. Ryan Sheremetta was justified in the shooting death of Kevin St. Arnaud.
The shooting took place in the early morning hours of Dec. 19, 2004 in Vanderhoof. St. Arnaud had robbed a pharmacy in the Vanderhoof mall, and fled into a nearby soccer field.
When Sheremetta pursued him, St. Arnaud turned and rushed at him. Sheremetta fired three shots, which hit St. Arnaud in the hand and chest, killing him.

Commission chairman Paul Kennedy released his final report Wednesday, which found Sheremetta fired in self defence. However, Kennedy's report outlined a number of concerns with how the RCMP investigation of the incident was handled.
Kennedy found that some aspects of the investigation into St. Arnaud's death were inadequate and lacked impartiality.
RCMP deputy criminal operations officer Chief Superintendent Dick Bent said the RCMP has made changes to improve the investigation of police-involved deaths.

"The CPC report makes 30 recommendations. (But) none of the recommendations would have prevented the tragedy of Dec. 19, 2004," Bent said. "In order to foster public confidence, we have to show we embrace best practices."

Kennedy reported that the RCMP failed to secure and preserve the scene. In addition, Sheremetta's supervisor at the Vanderhoof detachment was involved in taking statements from him and a key witness, Const. Colleen Erickson.
In addition, Kennedy questioned the validity of the blood stain analysis and use-of-force expert used in the investigation.
In general, the major case management model used by the RCMP was not fully followed, he reported.
"There were some errors that occurred," Bent said. "(But) there is no discipline in this case. On the whole, the investigation was not fatally flawed."
Now all major case managers have to be accredited, Bent said.

In addition, police officers from outside police agencies are called in to observe the investigation of police-related incidents and the commission can appoint in independent supervisor to observe the investigation.

"The main thing is we bring in that independence. It's set up to ensure a complete and unbiased investigation," Bent said. "We're not adverse to a different process that would have an outside body investigate, but we don't have that in B.C."

The RCMP did a separate investigation into possible perjury by Sheremetta, who said he had fallen and was lying on his back when he fired. Testimony by Erickson -- and forensic evidence from the autopsy -- indicated that Sheremetta was on his feet in a shooting stance at the time.
"We did a complete separate investigation into the perjury allegations," Bent said.
Crown prosecutors reviewed the evidence, and recommended that no charges be laid, he added.
Sheremetta is back on duty with a detachment in the Interior of B.C., Bent said.
